analysis.one_liner: Overhauls the Superfund toxic-waste law, easing polluters' cleanup liability while adding new community participation and health programs.
analysis.headline: Passed favorably out of two Senate committees in 1994 and was placed on the Senate calendar, but never received a floor vote before the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the 1980 Superfund law, which makes polluters pay to clean up the nation's worst toxic-waste sites. It would give communities near contaminated sites new rights to be informed and consulted, pay for health studies and citizen information offices, and add an environmental justice focus to site selection. At the same time, it would replace much of the polluter-pays lawsuit system with a negotiated allocation of shares, exempt many smaller contributors, banks, recyclers, and prospective property buyers from liability, cap what municipal-waste arrangers owe at 10% of cleanup costs, make the federal government pay for 'orphan shares' left by insolvent polluters, and set up a fund—financed by new taxes and assessments on insurers—to settle cleanup coverage disputes. It would also extend the Superfund cleanup program and its dedicated corporate environmental taxes.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities living near Superfund sites gain new Community Working Groups, citizen information offices, health assessments, and possible alternate water supplies or relocation help. Small businesses, municipalities, nonprofit groups, prospective property buyers, banks and lenders, recyclers, and railroads gain broad exemptions or caps on cleanup liability. States gain authority to run cleanups themselves with federal financing. Insurers and the companies they insure gain a new government fund that settles their coverage disputes. The environmental cleanup industry gains from extended federal funding, voluntary cleanup grants, and redevelopment loan subsidies.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near toxic sites, small businesses, banks

how_it_helps.text: Requires early, direct, and meaningful community involvement in every significant phase of a Superfund response, and lets 50 citizens or 20% of a community petition for a Community Working Group that EPA must consult at each stage [S3][S4][S5].

Creates independent Citizen Information and Access Offices in every affected state and tribal land, plus ombudsman offices in EPA's environmental justice office and regional offices, to tell residents about sites, their legal rights, and relocation or alternative water supply options [S3][S4][S5].

Directs federal priority-setting to account for communities exposed to hazardous substances through subsistence, religious, or cultural practices, requires interviews with affected residents, and prioritizes facilities in areas with environmental justice concerns [S3][S4].

Gives small businesses, municipalities, and individuals who arranged only municipal waste disposal expedited settlements, and caps at 10% of costs what such arrangers owe when that is their only liability [S3][S4].

Replaces much of the litigation over who pays for a cleanup with a 180-day allocation process before a neutral allocator, with a moratorium on lawsuits in the meantime, and lets the federal government cover 'orphan shares' left by insolvent polluters [S3][S4].
Extends the Superfund program's funding authorizations through FY 1999 and extends the corporate environmental income tax and Superfund financing rate through tax years before 2001 [S2][S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers bear new obligations: the federal government must pay for orphan shares 'backed by the full faith and credit of the United States,' reimburse parties whose innovative cleanup technology fails, finance voluntary cleanup grants and subsidized redevelopment loans, and fund the citizen participation offices. Corporations pay extended environmental taxes through 2001. Insurers pay new environmental insurance resolution taxes and assessments to capitalize the dispute-resolution fund. Polluters not covered by the new exemptions remain liable, and settling parties pay premiums covering remedy-failure and litigation risks.

drawbacks.text: The bill lets the President select cleanup remedies that do not meet federal or state standards under certain conditions, removes requirements that remedial actions conform to state standards, and replaces the current cleanup framework with a single numerical health risk level that can be waived as technically infeasible or unreasonably costly [S3][S4].

Broad liability exemptions—for lenders, fiduciaries, railroads, recyclers, small-quantity waste arrangers, and federal banking agencies—shift cleanup costs away from those parties and toward the Superfund and remaining liable polluters; the federal government also commits to paying orphan shares with the full faith and credit of the United States [S3][S4].

The Environmental Insurance Resolution Fund pays polluters to settle insurance coverage disputes and stays all pending coverage litigation, while penalizing polluters who litigate and do worse than the Fund's offer by making them pay 40% of the insurer's fees—outcomes insurance scholars and consumer advocates warned could favor insurers over policyholders [S3][S4].
States that take over cleanup authority must pay 15% of response costs, and a state may only impose cleanup standards stricter than federal law if it pays the incremental cost itself [S2][S3][S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The community participation, environmental justice, and health-provision titles are genuine gains for people living near contaminated sites, and the allocation process addresses a real problem—endless litigation over who pays. But the bill's liability carve-outs, capped municipal-waste liability, relaxed cleanup standards, and open-ended federal commitment to pay orphan shares move real cleanup costs from polluters onto taxpayers and could leave some sites less thoroughly cleaned. The insurance fund resolves a decades-long coverage dispute largely at public expense. Weighing it honestly: mixed, with real public benefits and real public costs.

outcome.mechanism: Both the Environment and Public Works and Finance committees approved it and it was placed on the Senate's calendar of pending business in September 1994, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

narrative.text: Sen. Max Baucus introduced the bill 'by request' on February 7, 1994, joined by Sen. Frank Lautenberg as the bill's only cosponsor [S5][S6][S7].

The Senate referred it first to the Environment and Public Works Committee, with instructions that once reported it go to the Finance Committee for matters in its jurisdiction, under a February 7 order [S7].

The Superfund, Recycling subcommittee held hearings on February 10, March 2, and April 12, and approved a substitute amendment favorably on June 14; the full committee held hearings June 28 and ordered the bill reported on August 3 [S7].
The Environment and Public Works Committee reported the bill with an amendment on August 19 (Report 103-349), with additional, minority, and supplemental views filed [S7].

The Finance Committee held hearings September 14 and reported the bill with a further amendment on September 30 (Report 103-389), with additional and minority views filed; the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 702 the same day [S5][S7].
No floor action ever followed; the Congress ended January 3, 1995, with the bill still on the calendar [S1][S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one's cleanup obligations changed. The polluters, banks, and insurers who would have gained liability relief and a government-funded dispute mechanism got nothing, but communities near toxic sites also got none of the new participation rights, health programs, or cleanup protections; the existing liability and litigation regime simply continued.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one—the cleanup rules stayed exactly as they were

sides.party_line_note: There was no floor vote to measure party splits. Both Senate committees—each chaired by a Democrat—reported the bill favorably, but Republican minority members filed additional and minority views at both committee reports, and only one Democrat signed on as cosponsor.

industries.industry: Chemical manufacturers and other polluting companies (Superfund 'potentially responsible parties')
industries.note: The bill creates an allocation process in place of much cleanup litigation, grants contribution protection and covenants not to sue to settling parties, caps municipal-waste arrangers at 10% of costs, and exempts many small-quantity contributors. Those savings come at the expense of fuller polluter-pays recovery, though the bill declares it does not change the core principles of retroactive, strict, joint and several liability.

industries.industry: Banks, lenders, and federal banking agencies
industries.note: Lender liability is capped at the 'actual benefit' gained from a cleanup, fiduciary liability is limited to assets held in trust, and Federal Deposit Insurance Act amendments absolve federal banking agencies of strict liability for contaminated property taken in receivership—shifting those cleanup costs to the Superfund and other parties.

A new Environmental Insurance Resolution Fund, financed by new taxes and assessments on insurers, pays polluters to settle coverage disputes and stays pending coverage litigation—an unusual intervention in insurer-policyholder disputes—but insurers gain an end to decades of coverage litigation and fee-shifting against policyholders who litigate and do worse than the Fund's offer.

The bill absolves arrangers of recycling transactions and railroads of cleanup liability if they meet compliance and reasonable-care conditions, ending their exposure under the old arrangement-for-disposal rules.

The bill extends Superfund authorizations through FY 1999, funds voluntary cleanup grants and subsidized redevelopment loans, reimburses parties for innovative cleanup technologies that fail, and creates a federal facility demonstration program for remediation technologies—keeping a federally funded cleanup pipeline flowing to the industry.

industries.industry: Property developers and prospective purchasers of contaminated sites
industries.note: Bona fide prospective purchasers and owners of contiguous contaminated property are absolved of liability and can receive assurances of no enforcement action, encouraging redevelopment of brownfield sites while cleanup costs fall on the fund and remaining liable parties.
